payload.title: Spike: ESP32-C3 board and compressed-instruction decoding
payload.description:
One-day spike, after Course 4 (not before W8). Pick a small ESP32-C3 board flashable from Chrome over Web Serial; measure the build image size (does the toolchain fit the runner image, or is a second task image acceptable); decide whether to add compressed (16-bit, C extension) decoding to the explorer. Related: M12 SIE-0ad8dc, SIE-60b608, SIE-4916e4.

Acceptance:
- a written decision recorded as a Kanbus comment: board chosen, image size measured, compressed decoding yes or no
- a flash of a bare-metal image from the browser demonstrated or ruled out
- no lesson work starts before this decision

Guardian decisions (all eight recommended answers accepted), from docs/real-machine-curriculum.md section 8:
1. She may see one line of read-only C in Course 1 (c1/10). It is the bridge the arc stands on and costs no typing.
2. In lesson text the two machines are called 'the RISC-V machine' (emulator; an exact model, not a toy) and 'the cloud computer' (Fargate). Never 'simulator', 'fake' or 'practice'.
3. Assume a laptop with a keyboard from Course 2 on. Course 1 works on a tablet; no touch editor is built.
4. A pre-warmed cloud task for up to 20 idle minutes before a cloud lesson is acceptable (the cost is cents).
5. No hard daily cap on cloud hours while there is one student and an allowlist; revisit if a second student joins.
6. Capstones allow any rule she chooses, including overflow or off the 16 x 16 screen; overflow and clipping become exhibits with a plain note, not an error.
7. No Rust lessons in this span; offer one side room after c4/05, 'f in Rust' (/explain already supports it).
8. ESP32-C3 comes after Course 4. Start with a one-day spike on a small board flashable from Chrome over Web Serial; the spike also measures build image size and decides whether to add compressed-instruction decoding to the explorer (the C3 runs 16-bit instructions by default).
